messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Liam, a 29-year-old Coast Guard serviceman, came to treatment several months after being mugged on his way home from an evening shift. He had parked a few blocks from his apartment, still in partial uniform, and was cutting through a dim stretch of sidewalk with his duffel over one shoulder when two men approached him. What he remembered most clearly was not a full sequence but sharp, disjointed fragments: the scrape of a shoe on concrete, one man stepping too close, the sudden movement of a hand toward his chest, the metallic flash of something he still could not confidently identify, his bag being yanked hard enough to twist him sideways. When he tried to describe the assault in session, he kept stopping and restarting. He would get as far as “they came up on my left” and then lose the thread, frowning as if the rest were sealed off behind something he could sense but not reach. He said more than once that he “just can’t put it into words right,” and the effort of trying seemed to leave him frustrated and vaguely ashamed.

In the days after the robbery, Liam gave statements to police and to his supervisor because his Coast Guard ID had been in the stolen bag. Each time he was asked to recount what happened, he was struck by how little of it felt like a normal memory. It did not come back as a coherent story with a beginning, middle, and end. Instead there were isolated bits that arrived without order: the pressure in his throat when he realized he could not immediately call for help, the smell of wet pavement, his own hand on the strap of the bag, the image of one attacker’s jawline under a hood. Other stretches were simply absent. He could tell there had been shouting, but could not reliably say who said what. He knew he had ended up on the ground, but not exactly how. This patchwork quality unnerved him, because he was used to being observant and precise in his work, and he could feel himself searching for connections that never settled into place.

What was equally strange to him was that sometimes he could talk about the mugging with no feeling at all. Sitting with his girlfriend in their kitchen or answering a routine question from a superior, he would hear himself describing being robbed in a flat, distant voice, as if he were reciting something that had happened to another man. He noticed the mismatch and found it unsettling. He knew the event should feel frightening or enraging, yet at moments it seemed remote, drained of emotion, and this emotional deadness made the whole thing harder for him to understand. At other times a single fragment would surface—a hand grabbing his uniform, the instant of realizing he was outnumbered—without any fuller context around it.

His work in the Coast Guard gave these difficulties a particular edge. He was accustomed to clear reporting, chain of events, practical detail. On base, when colleagues spoke casually about theft in the city or asked whether the police had found anything, he felt exposed by how incomplete his own account remained. He could say the facts in outline, but the actual memory would not organize itself. Driving in for duty before dawn, he sometimes found himself replaying disconnected images rather than a narrative, almost as if his mind had stored snapshots instead of an experience. The result was less a story he could tell than a set of sensory shards he carried around with him.

By the time he sought help, Liam was exhausted by this ongoing sense that the worst night of his adult life existed in him only as broken pieces and blank spaces. His girlfriend had encouraged him after another evening when he tried to explain what he remembered and stopped midway, rubbing his forehead and saying, “It doesn’t come out right. It’s like I only have parts.” What frightened him most was not only the robbery itself, but the persistence of this altered remembering—how often the event felt both inaccessible and strangely impersonal. He wanted help making sense of what had happened, and he hoped that if the memory could finally become something whole and sayable, it would stop feeling like a series of disconnected scenes belonging to someone else.
